citation.title: Scaling and logic in the color code on a superconducting quantum processor
citation.arxiv: arXiv:2412.14256 (v1, 18 Dec 2024; HTML + LaTeX source used here)
citation.note: Author list abbreviated; quotes below are from the arXiv v1 HTML, LaTeX math rendered as plain text (e.g. '$35\text{\,}\mathrm{ns}$' -> '35 ns').

device.name: Willow (72 qubits)
device.quote: We implement this logical qubit on the 72-qubit Willow processor first introduced in Ref. 3
device.section: II Color codes with superconducting qubits
device.qubits_used_quote: We use 37 qubits of a 72-qubit quantum processor to encode the distance-five logical qubit, and three 13-qubits subsets to encode the distance-three logical qubits.
device.qubits_used_section: App. D.2 Color Code Location on Processor
device.coordinate_convention: (row, col) as in the Zenodo QUBIT_COORDS and the axes of Fig. 8; grid = 72 qubits, row r spans cols lo..hi: {"0": [5, 5], "1": [4, 6], "2": [3, 7], "3": [2, 8], "4": [1, 9], "5": [0, 10], "6": [0, 10], "7": [1, 9], "8": [2, 8], "9": [3, 7], "10": [4, 6], "11": [5, 5]} (read from Fig. 8); nearest-neighbour square-grid couplers.
device.connectivity_quote: This choice is particularly attractive for superconducting qubits because it only requires nearest-neighbor connectivity on a square grid of qubits.
device.readout_lines_quote: The design of this processor favors the simultaneous readout of all qubits sharing a readout line to minimize measurement-induced dephasing.
device.memory_patch_note: Roles derived from the Zenodo circuits: data = measured only at the end, aux = measured every cycle; reset-only qubits are reset each cycle but never gated or measured (purpose not stated in the paper); d3_east lists (5,8) in QUBIT_COORDS but never touches it.
device.teleport_layout_note: Figure-to-chip placement is OUR choice (paper gives no chip coordinates for the teleportation experiment): same orientation as Fig. 5/15, translated to fit the 72-qubit grid, maximizing overlap with the paper's d=5 patch, then closest to chip centre.

single_qubit_pi.quote: π-rotations and π/2-rotations have durations of 35 ns and 18 ns, respectively.
single_qubit_pi.section: App. B Device and Experimental Setup

single_qubit_pi_over_2.quote: π-rotations and π/2-rotations have durations of 35 ns and 18 ns, respectively.
single_qubit_pi_over_2.section: App. B Device and Experimental Setup

single_qubit_z.quote: We implement single-qubit gates using microwave DRAG pulses [7] for X rotations and virtual Z gates [8].
single_qubit_z.section: App. B Device and Experimental Setup
single_qubit_z.note: virtual Z = frame update, zero duration (standard meaning; the paper gives no number)

cz.quote: These CZ gates have a duration of 37 ns.
cz.section: App. B Device and Experimental Setup
cz.mechanism_quote: Controlled-Z (CZ) gates between neighboring qubits are realized by tuning the transition frequencies of the two qubits such that the |11> state is resonant with the |20> state, while also adjusting the frequency of a tunable coupler to control the coupling strength.

readout.quote: The readout protocol, including cavity depletion time, lasts for 600 ns.
readout.section: App. B Device and Experimental Setup
readout.note: includes resonator depletion; frequency-multiplexed dispersive readout

reset.quote: Following readout, we perform a 160-ns multi-level reset as described in Ref. 6.
reset.section: App. B Device and Experimental Setup

dqlr.quote: For state preservation experiments, we also include a data qubit leakage removal (DQLR) procedure lasting 53 ns.
dqlr.section: App. B Device and Experimental Setup

qec_cycle.quote: The total error correction cycle duration after decomposition and optimization is approximately 1.3 µs.
qec_cycle.applies_to: memory (state-preservation) circuits after the readout-line transformation

dynamical_decoupling.quote: During the auxiliary qubit measurement and reset (steps 19 and 1), we apply an XY4 dynamical decoupling sequence [20] on all data qubits. After the auxiliary qubit resets, we also apply data-qubit leakage removal (DQLR) [21].

derived_cycle_check.formula: 7 H layers x 18 ns + 10 CZ layers x 37 ns + 600 ns readout + 160 ns reset + 53 ns DQLR
derived_cycle_check.derivation: layer counts from the Zenodo memory circuits (verify.py B); assumes each H layer costs one pi/2 pulse (18 ns) and that the two R layers per cycle in the files are one 160 ns reset; DD/idle layers not separately timed
derived_cycle_check.status: OUR derivation, consistent with the quoted ~1.3 us; not a paper statement

derived_teleport_cycle_estimate.formula: <= 9 H layers x 18 ns + 8 CZ layers x 37 ns + 600 ns + 160 ns (no DQLR: App. B states it for state preservation)
derived_teleport_cycle_estimate.status: OUR estimate for the CNOT circuit as drawn in Fig. 15 (8 CNOT layers per cycle, H+CZ compilation assumed); the paper states no duration for the teleportation cycles

electronics.quote: The device is installed at the bottom of a dilution refrigerator [4] and wired to custom room-temperature electronics for control.
electronics.section: App. B Device and Experimental Setup
electronics.control_lines_quote: We use a single control line per flux-tunable transmon [5] qubit to realize single-qubit gates and to tune the transition frequency to implement two-qubit gates and multi-level reset [6].
electronics.readout_quote: Qubit states are read out dispersively by applying frequency-multiplexed microwave pulses.

decoding.mode: offline (inferred; not stated as a word): the neural decoder is fine-tuned on experimental data, the MLE decoder is ~1000x slower than Chromobius, and Chromobius is called only a candidate for future real-time decoding; frame updates for teleportation are applied in post-processing
decoding.decoders_quote: In this work, we explore three decoders for the color code: a möbius decoder (Chromobius) [2], a most-likely-error (MLE) decoder, and a neural-network decoder (AlphaQubit) [24].
decoding.realtime_quote: This makes Chromobius a promising candidate for real-time decoding in the near future.
decoding.speed_quote: After training, AlphaQubit can decode at an intermediate speed which is about 3 times slower than Chromobius, but 300 times faster than the MLE decoder.
decoding.mle_quote: The most-likely error is found by mapping the decoding problem onto a mixed-integer program [28, 29, Supp. 1A] which is solved with the High Performance Optimization Software (HiGHS) package [30].
decoding.teleport_decoder_quote: For state teleportation, a single instance of AlphaQubit processes the syndrome elements from both logical qubits in each cycle, along with additional syndrome elements corresponding to the stabilizers at the interface of the logical qubits during the merge cycles.
decoding.postprocessing_quote: The parity measurement outcome m1 and L1’s Z-basis measurement outcome m2 are used in post-processing to apply a conditional Pauli frame update Z_L^m1 X_L^m2 to the state of L2
decoding.postprocessing_section: VI State teleportation using lattice surgery

results.quote: With a neural-network decoder (AlphaQubit) [24], we obtain Λ3/5=1.56(4) and ε5=0.0110(2).

results.what: eps_3 averaged d=3 logical error per cycle
results.quote: This is significantly lower than the logical error per cycle, ε̄3=0.0171(3), underscoring the efficiency of implementing transversal single-qubit gates.
Experimentally, we observe Λ3/5=1.53(4), ε̄3=0.0176(3) and ε̄5=0.0115(2), using the same MLE decoder.
The observed error suppression factor is in reasonable agreement with the simulated error suppression factor Λ3/5^sim=1.680(4).
As expected, weight-6 stabilizers exhibit a higher error detection probability (pd,6=0.149 when averaging over all cycles and stabilizers), compared to boundary weight-4 stabilizers (pd,4=0.112)
Using logical randomized benchmarking [38], we find that transversal Clifford gates add an error of only 0.0027(3), which is substantially less than the error of an idling error correction cycle.
obtaining an average infidelity of 0.039(3) using the Möbius decoder (Chromobius) [2] and 0.009(4) when post-selecting for runs without detectable errors (keeping on average 74.8 % of the runs)
Calculating fidelity with the ideal logical states yields fidelities between 86.5(1) % and 90.7(1) % when decoded with the neural-network decoder (Fig. 5k).
results.section: VI State teleportation using lattice surgery

results.quote: These measurements enable us to bound the average fidelity of the single-qubit teleportation channel, T, at F(T) ≥ 84.7(1) %
results.section: VI State teleportation using lattice surgery

results.quote: We then perform the M_XX parity measurement, which involves a three-cycle lattice surgery merge operation, followed by a split operation over one cycle
results.section: VI State teleportation using lattice surgery

results.quote: In the first merge cycle, two new X-basis stabilizers are added, indicated by the hatched tiles in Fig. 5d. In addition, the green (red) boundary stabilizers of L1 (L2) are expanded from weight-four to weight-six stabilizers in both bases, requiring the addition of two data qubits initially prepared in a Bell state.
results.section: VI State teleportation using lattice surgery

results.quote: The M_XX parity outcome is the product of the two interface X stabilizers and the additional data qubit read out in the X basis.
results.section: App. I.1 State Teleportation Circuit Details

results.quote: At present, the surface code achieves better logical error suppression (on the same processor, Λsc3/5=2.31(2) [3])
We observe that the threshold at which the logical error per cycle for the higher distances intersect is around pth≈0.005 (see Fig. 11).

Each experiment is repeated 5 000 times for 10 different initialization bitstrings: five are randomly chosen and the remaining five are their binary complements, thereby ensuring equal representation of both eigenstates for odd-distance codes.
